entries.title: Daisy One Review: Comfy and Tactile Headphones
entries.summary: The company’s first headphones look very stylish and have great tactile features but underwhelm on sound quality.
entries.content:
Buttons! Knobs! No touch controls! Elegant. Good build quality. Comfy fit. Great battery life. Cheaper than the (flagship) competition.

TIRED

Sound quality is fine. Just fine. Noise canceling is bad, and transparency mode is worse.

I wish the Daisy One headphones sounded as nice as they look.

The Daisy One is the first pair of headphones from Daisy, a California company that employs engineers formerly from the Samsung-owned audio company Harman Professional Solutions. Together with a sound system developed by Utah-based ((nxc)) systems, the Daisy One is attempting to burst its way into a very saturated premium audio market Kool-Aid-Man style, with a focus on design and tactical buttons.

You’ve probably seen the ads for these headphones on Instagram. They seemed pervasive on social media, at least for a little while, vying for eyeballs as they enter an industry dominated by massive companies like Sony, Apple, and Bose. By focusing on design, Daisy wants to go head-to-head with premium headphone manufacturers that make the best headphones. The Daisies are gorgeous, comfy, and at $349, definitely cheaper than many other options. But if you’re an audiophile or stickler for sound quality, you’re probably better off saving your money for something else.

Before the product launched, Daisy CEO Jack Mulroe said the motivation for making Daisy was a lack of differentiation in headphones. He believes the market has been stale since Beats by Dre blew up with its very colorful (now Apple-owned) headsets. That said, the first wave of Daisy headphones comes in just three colors: Silver, Pacific (blue), and Kelp (greenish brown). I’ve been demoing a pair of the Pacific blues and genuinely like wearing them. The build quality is great. An array of aluminum and TR90 polymers makes these feel top shelf.

The Daisy One comes in a very nice box that Mulroe says is meant to feel like a book you’d place on a library shelf. It is nice, but I’m going to gently accuse the company of preying on the millennial need to hoard empty boxes, certain they’ll need them later. The included carrying case is a smooth, equally elegant lump that snaps closed with a magnetic latch.

The headphones are slightly heavier than some of the other primo cans on the market, but the earpads’ soft cushions work really well to squish around glasses. I can keep them on for hours at a time and not feel the need to pull them off. But they’re not so lightweight that I tend to forget I’m wearing them, unlike my pair of Sony WH-1000XM4s. The earcups magnetically attach, so they pop off easily if you need to replace them.

The Daisies do have a bit of heft, but that also translates into a tactility that other, more plasticky headphones don’t convey. They also last a long time, rated at 45 hours of battery life. I never had a problem with having to recharge them. The headphones have a 3.5-mm aux port and a USB-C audio connection that supports 24-bit digital audio at 44.1 kHz or 48 kHz. After the product launched, Daisy said it signed paperwork with Sony to release LDAC support, Sony’s high-res Bluetooth codec, via an over-the-air update later this year.

The volume dial is easily the best part of the Daisy headphones. Maybe one of the best dials on any headphones, especially in this price range. It’s a scored metal knob that rolls very smoothly. Press the side to pause or play the music with a very satisfying click. Double-click to skip a song, triple-tap to go one track back. It’s very straightforward.

Long-press the active noise cancellation button behind the dial to activate Still Mode, where a series of Daisy’s on-device relaxing soundscapes take over. You can switch between soft, ambient water-based sounds that Daisy says are recorded across California, such as rainfall, a forest stream, a waterfall, and ocean waves. There is also a five-minute breathwork session that sounds much less wet. It's all very zen, and a nice feature to be able to quickly swap to when you need to chill out.

The headphones do not incorporate any touch controls, which is a godsend. There is no accidentally pausing or triggering an AI assistant when you’re just trying to change the volume. You can switch between noise canceling and transparency modes with the press of a button.

The problem? The noise canceling and transparency modes are not very good. Walking out when it’s windy or sitting on a loud subway train going underground is almost worse with noise canceling on, as it distorts the sound into sharp, loud blasts. Transparency mode just doesn’t let much sound in from the outside and distorts the audio quality. These features aren’t great, though Daisy says it’s aware of the issue and is aiming to fix it with software updates over time. But you should never buy a product based on the promises of future software updates.

The companion app is simple to use, which is nice, but the sound choices are underwhelming. It comes default on a mode called Daisy EQ, with a dynamic bass feature turned on. That works well enough for bass-heavy EDM, though it does sound noticeably muddier than my Sony WH-1000XM4. Switching the EQ to a flat sound profile reveals the real weakness of these headphones. The sound quality just feels more hollow than it should, with highs sounding tinny and the lows coming across as very unenthusiastic without the dynamic bass setting on. (Call quality is fine, and nobody on the other end of a call said I came through weird.)

That’s probably the sacrifice you have to make when trying to save a couple of hundred bucks over top-tier headphones. But the Daisies are also cheaper than they could have been. When the company announced the product, it listed the price at $399. Now, it has dropped to $349.

I do want to point out that you can find top-end headphones, like Sony’s latest WH-1000XM6 or Bose’s QuietComfort Ultra 2, for close to the price of the Daisy One headphones during sale events (the XM6’s have dropped as low as $378 last month, and the Bose are $370 right now as of publication).

The hardware feels great, which has me intrigued about what the company will do next. Sadly, the One just ain’t quite it yet.

entries.title: SJY Zeph Open-Back Headphones Review: Music Through Magnets
entries.summary: SJY’s Zeph are brilliant wired headphones, using flippable earcups for two different takes on your favorite music.
entries.content:
Fun and unique handmade headphones. Comfortable. Lively sound with exquisite detail. Should prove durable as the minimalist design means fewer parts to degrade or break.

TIRED

Relatively heavy. The 4.4mm balanced jack requires a powerful headphone amp most people won’t already own.

How much of a difference can the earpads on a set of headphones really make? The idea of getting a noticeable sonic difference based on the size and shape of thin pieces of foam under leather or velour sounds like audiophile snake oil.

As a fan of vintage electrostatic headphones, I’ve confidently operated under this belief by chintzing out and buying replacement earpads of roughly the right size and shape rather than ponying up $100 or more for OEM. It never occurred to me that this might have been a mistake until I tested SJY’s new Zeph open-backed planar magnetic headphones.

The end result is far from a gimmick—they’re among my favorite pair of headphones of all the ones I’ve ever used.

Magnetic Sound

Most consumer headphones and speakers reproduce sound by vibrating a cone using a wire coil. But the Zeph is different. It’s a planar magnetic headphone, which means it uses a magnetic field to vibrate a flat, thin diaphragm to reproduce sound. These have a faster and more accurate sound but are generally thought to sacrifice some punch on lower bass frequencies. Planar magnetics are a growing category that is expected to more than double in the next decade—even if these headphones remain niche today.

I’ve owned a few pairs of planar magnetics and am generally a fan because I like loads of detail in my music. True to form, the Zeph has exceptional detail and frequently delivers the hyper-real quality I look for in headphones of this range. It aced my favorite reference test, which is being able to hear Keith Moon move around on a squeaky stool during the opening of “Won't Get Fooled Again.” On Radiohead’s “Daydreaming” from A Moon Shaped Pool, the glockenspiel pierces through the piano and loops with a shimmery quality. Listen closely, and you can hear the metronome in the left channel (and that’s all with the less-detailed holes-in-front orientation). The precision and texture here is unprecedented. Meanwhile, there is plenty of low-end for my taste—I get a thick, bouncy bass when clicking forward to “Identikit.”

Note, though, that planar magnetic headphones generally require more amplification than standard headphones, and the Zeph is relatively power-hungry. It will demand at least a watt per channel, or preferably more. I have a handful of headphone amps and DAC dongles lying around, but only one device that can drive the Zephs. That’s a Creative Soundblaster X5 that has a balanced 4.4-mm headphone port. The 4.4-mm port is pretty standard on audiophile equipment these days, but it’s worth a warning to regular folks who are accustomed to standard 3.5-mm and 6.3-mm headphone jacks. You won’t be able to buy these headphones and plug them into even a standard stereo receiver.

Thin Mint

The Zeph’s magnetic earpads are flippable, with one side having pinprick-thick microperforations and the other being smooth. You can tweak the sonic signature by swapping the seam from down to up. If the size with holes is in front of your ear, the tuning becomes slightly colder and wider, with added pop to instruments. Flip the pads over so that the millimeter-thick holes are behind your ear and the sound signature is a tad warmer and more cohesive, with mixes sounding more blended.

The disparity is relatively subtle—like the difference between a martini that’s stirred (holes in front) as opposed to shaken (holes in the back)—but it’s definitely audible. I tend to prefer headphones with an expansive soundstage and lots of detail. Though with the SJY, I find the slightly warmer and more natural sound more inviting for long listening sessions. And these are headphones that can live comfortably on your head for long stretches.

The impact of the simple switch of earpad orientation is made possible partly because of the design’s arch minimalism. The design was intended to have as few pieces as possible and to hold them rigidly in place with the goal of achieving purity of sound. The aluminum chassis, diaphragm, and driver all measure low, single-digit millimeters. The entire body that clips onto the pads combined is only as thick as a typical monthly magazine in 2026.

Because of that, these headphones feel more like a carbon steel pocketknife in the hand than a pair of ANC Bluetooth headphones. They have an impressive sturdiness and don’t feel like something you’ll worry about breaking if you fall asleep with them on. They do weigh more than a pound—at 570 grams with their cable, they’re almost 40 percent heavier than AirPods Max. They come with a padded case that has a generous layer of foam for protection and a braided cable.

Despite their relative heft, I’ve had them perched on my head very consistently since the testers arrived. That’s mainly due to the detailed sound they render from the many gigs of too rarely used 24-bit Hi-Res FLACs on my desktop, as headphones like this can make old songs sound new again. And if it starts to sound old again? Just flip those earpads to have the holes on the other side, and it’s a whole new ballgame.

Curve Killers

The flippable earpads are also made possible by the way they’ve been tuned. High-end wired headphones are having a bit of a renaissance, growing slowly while the rest of the audiophile market dies off around them. But they are also getting more homogenized. That’s because the major makers are aiming to tune their products along the Harman Curve, a guideline for the ideal earphone frequency response built from extensive scientific research, including blind listening.

While the Harman Curve is controversial among enthusiasts on message boards, it’s been widely adopted by headphone makers who strive to get their stock tuning on target. SJY doesn’t reject the Harman Curve but has tweaked the tuning away from it and, even more interestingly, intentionally allows a listener to switch up the signature depending on the orientation of the earpads. That’s what makes them so unique in a world saturated with headphone options. After all, SJY is first and foremost an enthusiast brand, owned and operated by Jeffrey Yin, who started the company in 2020 on the day after his 18th birthday. The SJY line has four models so far, with a fifth on the way, all made by Yin himself in Houston. You don’t buy these to have just another pair of headphones. We hope that’s obvious enough.

But for me, it’s as close to a perfect pair of headphones as I’ve ever owned.
